text: Rachel Louise Carson (May 27, 1907 – April 14, 1964) was an American marine biologist, writer, and conservationist whose sea trilogy (1941–1955) and book Silent Spring (1962) are credited with advancing marine conservation and the global environmental movement. Born on May 27, 1907, on a family farm near Springdale, Pennsylvania, by the Allegheny River near Pittsburgh, she was the daughter of Maria Frazier (McLean) and Robert Warden Carson, an insurance salesman. She spent much time exploring her family's 65-acre (26 ha) farm and began writing stories involving animals at age eight, with her first story published at ten. She enjoyed reading St. Nicholas Magazine, works by Beatrix Potter, Gene Stratton-Porter, and later Herman Melville, Joseph Conrad, and Robert Louis Stevenson, with the natural world—especially the ocean—being a common theme. Carson attended Springdale’s small school through tenth grade and graduated in 1925 at the top of her class of 44 students. She enrolled at Pennsylvania College for Women (now Chatham University) in Pittsburgh, initially studying English before switching to biology in January 1928. She continued contributing to the school’s student newspaper and literary supplement. Admitted to Johns Hopkins University in 1928, she was forced to remain at the college for her senior year due to financial difficulties and graduated magna cum laude in 1929. After a summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory, she continued her studies in zoology and genetics at Johns Hopkins, becoming a part-time student and assistant in Raymond Pearl’s laboratory, where she worked with rats and Drosophila to earn tuition. After false starts with pit vipers and squirrels, she completed a dissertation on the embryonic development of the pronephros (urinary organ) in fish. In June 1932, she earned a master’s degree in zoology and intended to pursue a doctorate, but in 1934, she left Johns Hopkins to seek a full-time teaching position due to financial hardship during the Great Depression. Her father died suddenly in 1935, worsening her family’s financial situation and leaving her to care for her aging mother. With the encouragement of her undergraduate biology mentor Mary Scott Skinker, Carson secured a temporary position with the U.S. Bureau of Fisheries, where she wrote radio copy for a series of 52 seven-minute educational broadcasts called Romance Under the Waters, focused on aquatic life. She also began submitting articles on marine life in the Chesapeake Bay to local newspapers and magazines. She earned extra income as a lecturer at the University of Maryland’s Dental and Pharmacy Schools and Johns Hopkins University. Her supervisor, impressed by the success of the radio series, asked her to write the introduction to a public brochure and later secured her the first full-time position at the Bureau, which she obtained in 1936 by outscoring all other applicants in the civil service exam, becoming the second woman hired by the Bureau of Fisheries as a junior aquatic biologist. Using her research and consultations with marine biologists, she wrote a steady stream of articles for The Baltimore Sun and other publications. In 1937, her older sister died, leaving her as the sole breadwinner for her mother and two nieces. In July 1937, the Atlantic Monthly published a revised version of an essay, The World of Waters, originally written for a brochure, as Undersea, a vivid narrative of a journey along the ocean floor. This marked a major turning point in her writing career. Simon & Schuster, impressed by Undersea, suggested she expand it into a book, leading to the publication of Under the Sea Wind (1941), which received excellent reviews but sold poorly. Her article-writing success continued with features in Sun Magazine, Nature, and Collier’s. In 1945, Carson first encountered DDT, a revolutionary pesticide dubbed the "insect bomb" after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, which was only beginning to undergo safety and ecological testing. Editors found the subject unappealing, and she published nothing on DDT until 1962. Carson rose within the Fish and Wildlife Service, becoming a supervisor of a small writing staff in 1945 and chief editor of publications in 1949, which allowed more fieldwork and freedom in choosing writing projects but also increased administrative duties. By 1948, she began transitioning to full-time writing and hired literary agent Marie Rodell, with whom she maintained a close professional relationship. Oxford University Press expressed interest in her book proposal for a life history of the ocean, prompting her to complete the manuscript of The Sea Around Us by early 1950. Chapters appeared in Science Digest and The Yale Review, with "The Birth of an Island" winning the American Association for the Advancement of Science’s George Westinghouse Science Writing Prize. Beginning in June 1951, nine chapters were serialized in The New Yorker. The book was published by Oxford University Press on July 2, 1951, remained on The New York Times Bestseller List for 86 weeks, was abridged by Reader’s Digest, won the 1952 National Book Award for Nonfiction and the John Burroughs Medal, and resulted in two honorary doctorates. She licensed a documentary film based on it, The Sea, which was successful and led to the republication of Under the Sea Wind, which became a bestseller. With success came financial security, allowing her to leave her job in 1952 to write full-time. She received numerous requests for speaking engagements, fan mail, and correspondence regarding The Sea Around Us, as well as work on the film script she had the right to review. She was dissatisfied with the final version of the script by Irwin Allen, describing it as "a cross between a believe-it-or-not and a breezy travelogue," and found it scientifically embarrassing. However, she had no control over the script’s content, leading to scientific inconsistencies. Despite her requests to correct these issues, Allen proceeded with the film, which won the 1953 Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. Carson was deeply embittered and never sold film rights to her work again. In the summer of 1953, she met Dorothy M. Freeman on Southport Island, Maine, beginning a devoted friendship that lasted the rest of her life. Their relationship was primarily conducted through letters and occasional physical contact, with over 12 years of correspondence totaling around 900 letters, many of which were published in the book Always, Rachel (1995) by Beacon Press. According to her biographer Linda J. Lear, Carson needed a devoted friend who would listen without advising and accept her wholly as both a writer and a woman, and she found this in Freeman. The two shared common interests, especially nature, and spent summers together in Maine. Commentators noted that their love was expressed almost entirely through letters and rare physical gestures. Freeman shared parts of Carson’s letters with her husband to help him understand the relationship, but much of the correspondence was carefully guarded. Some believe the relationship was romantic, with Carson writing, "But, oh darling, I want to be with you so terribly that it hurts!" and Freeman stating, "I love you beyond expression... My love is boundless as the Sea." Carson’s last letter to Freeman before her death ended with, "Never forget, dear one, how deeply I have loved you all these years." Shortly before her death, Carson and Freeman destroyed hundreds of letters. The surviving correspondence was published in 1995 as Always, Rachel: The Letters of Rachel Carson and Dorothy Freeman, 1952–1964: An Intimate Portrait of a Remarkable Friendship, edited by Martha Freeman, Dorothy’s granddaughter, who noted that early letters showed caution about romantic terminology, prompting the destruction of some letters within the first two years. One reviewer described the pair as fitting Carolyn Heilbrun’s characterization of a strong female friendship, where what matters is "not whether friends are homosexual or heterosexual, lovers or not, but whether they share the wonderful energy of work in the public sphere." There was a disagreement over Carson’s final arrangements: her brother Robert Carson insisted on burying her cremated remains beside their mother in Maryland, against her wish to be buried in Maine. A compromise was reached, with an organizing committee including her agent Marie Rodell, editor Paul Brooks, and Dorothy Freeman. In the spring of 1964, Dorothy received half of Rachel’s ashes from Robert Carson, and in the summer of that year, she scattered the ashes along the rocky shores of Sheepscot Bay in Maine. Early in 1953, Carson began library and field research on the ecology and organisms of the Atlantic shore. In 1955, she completed The Edge of the Sea, the third volume of her sea trilogy, focusing on life in coastal ecosystems, particularly along the Eastern Seaboard. It appeared in The New Yorker in two condensed installments before its October 26 book release by Houghton Mifflin. By this time, her reputation for clear and poetic prose was well established, though the book received favorable reviews, not quite as enthusiastic as The Sea Around Us. From 1955 to 1956, she worked on several projects, including a script for an Omnibus episode, "Something About the Sky," and wrote articles for popular magazines. Her planned next book on evolution was abandoned due to Julian Huxley’s Evolution in Action and her difficulty in finding a compelling approach. Instead, her focus turned to conservation, and she considered a book tentatively titled Remembrance of the Earth. She became involved with The Nature Conservancy and other conservation groups and planned to buy and preserve an area in Maine she and Freeman called the "Lost Woods." In early 1957, a family tragedy occurred when one of her nieces, whom she had cared for since the 1940s, died at age 31, leaving her 5-year-old son, Roger Christie, an orphan. Carson adopted Roger and took on the responsibility of caring for her aging mother, moving to Silver Spring, Maryland. In 1957, she worked on establishing a new living situation and studied specific environmental threats. By late 1957, Carson closely followed federal proposals for widespread pesticide spraying, including the USDA’s plan to eradicate fire ants and rising programs involving chlorinated hydrocarbons and organophosphates. For the rest of her life, her main professional focus was the dangers of pesticide overuse. Silent Spring, her most influential book, was published by Houghton Mifflin on September 27, 1962. The book described the harmful effects of pesticides on the environment and is widely credited with helping launch the environmental movement. Carson was not the first or only person to raise concerns about DDT, but her combination of scientific knowledge and poetic writing reached a broad audience and helped focus opposition to DDT use. The book’s publication as a mass-market paperback by Fawcett Crest in January 1964 expanded its reach. In 1994, an edition of Silent Spring was published with an introduction by Vice President Al Gore. In 2012, Silent Spring was designated a National Historic Chemical Landmark by the American Chemical Society for its role in the development of the modern environmental movement. Starting in the mid-1940s, Carson became concerned about synthetic pesticides, many developed through military-funded science since World War II. The 1957 U.S. government gypsy moth (now called spongy moth) eradication program, which involved aerial spraying of DDT and other pesticides mixed with fuel oil, including private land, prompted her to devote her research and next book to pesticides and environmental poisons. Landowners on Long Island filed a lawsuit to stop the spraying, and many followed the case closely. Though the suit was lost, the Supreme Court granted petitioners the right to gain injunctions against potential environmental damage in the future, laying the foundation for later environmental actions. The Audubon Naturalist Society also opposed such spraying and recruited Carson to publicize the government’s spraying practices and related research. Carson began a four-year project that would become Silent Spring by gathering examples of environmental damage from DDT. She attempted to enlist others, including essayist E. B. White and several journalists and scientists. By 1958, she had arranged a book deal with plans to co-write with Newsweek science journalist Edwin Diamond. However, when The New Yorker commissioned a long and well-paid article on the topic, she began considering writing more than just the introduction and conclusion, eventually turning it into a solo project (Diamond later wrote one of the harshest critiques of Silent Spring). As her research progressed, Carson found a community of scientists documenting the physiological and environmental effects of pesticides. She also used her connections with government scientists to obtain confidential information. From reading scientific literature and interviewing scientists, she identified two camps on pesticides: those who dismissed potential dangers without conclusive proof and those open to the possibility of harm and willing to consider alternatives like biological pest control. She also found significant support and evidence from a group of biodynamic agriculture organic market gardeners, their adviser Dr. Ehrenfried Pfeiffer, other contacts, and their legal actions (1957–1960) against the U.S. government. According to recent research by Paull (2013), this may have been the primary and (for strategic reasons) uncredited source for Carson’s book. Marjorie Spock and Mary T. Richards of Long Island, New York, contested the aerial spraying of DDT. They compiled evidence and shared it with Carson, who used it, their extensive contacts, and trial transcripts as primary input for Silent Spring. Carson described the content as "a gold mine of information" and said, "I feel guilty about the" (incomplete).

Rachel Carson benefited from her connections with numerous government scientists, who provided her with confidential information. Through reading scientific literature and interviewing experts, she identified two distinct scientific viewpoints on pesticides: those who rejected the possibility of harm without conclusive evidence, and those who acknowledged potential risks and supported alternative methods like biological pest control. She found strong support and substantial evidence from organic market gardeners, including their adviser Dr. Ehrenfried Pfeiffer, their contacts, and their legal actions (1957–1960) against the U.S. government; recent research by Paull (2013) suggests this group was the primary and uncredited source for her book. Marjorie Spock and Mary T. Richards of Long Island, New York, opposed aerial spraying of dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT), compiled evidence, and shared it with Carson, who used their findings, contacts, and trial transcripts as key material for Silent Spring. Carson described the material as "a gold mine of information" and expressed guilt over the volume of their contributions, citing multiple references to Pfeiffer and his correspondence. In 1959, the USDA's Agricultural Research Service responded to Carson’s criticism with the public service film Fire Ant on Trial, which she labeled "flagrant propaganda" for ignoring the dangers of pesticides like dieldrin and heptachlor to humans and wildlife. That same year, Carson wrote a letter published in The Washington Post linking the decline in bird populations—the "silencing of birds"—to pesticide overuse. This was also the year of the "Great Cranberry Scandal," when 1957–1959 U.S. cranberry crops were found to contain high levels of aminotriazole, a herbicide that causes cancer in lab rats, leading to the halt of all cranberry product sales. Carson attended FDA hearings on pesticide regulation and was discouraged by the aggressive tactics of chemical industry representatives, including expert testimony contradicted by the scientific literature she studied, and she questioned possible "financial inducements behind certain pesticide programs." Research at the Library of Medicine of the National Institutes of Health connected her to medical researchers studying cancer-causing chemicals, particularly Wilhelm Hueper of the National Cancer Institute, who classified many pesticides as carcinogens. With the help of research assistant Jeanne Davis and NIH librarian Dorothy Algire, Carson found evidence supporting the pesticide-cancer link; she viewed the toxicity of synthetic pesticides as clear-cut, though such conclusions were controversial outside a small group of scientists. By 1960, Carson had sufficient research material and was writing rapidly, having reviewed hundreds of individual pesticide exposure incidents and resulting human illness and ecological damage. However, a duodenal ulcer and infections kept her bedridden in January, delaying completion, and as she recovered in March, she discovered cysts in her left breast, one requiring a mastectomy. Though her doctor described the procedure as precautionary and recommended no further treatment, by December she learned the tumor was malignant and had metastasized. Her research was also delayed by revisions for a new edition of The Sea Around Us and a collaborative photo essay with Erich Hartmann. Most of the writing was completed by fall 1960, except for discussions on biological pest controls and investigations into a few new pesticides. Further health issues slowed final revisions in 1961 and early 1962. While writing, Carson concealed her illness to prevent pesticide companies from using it against her, fearing they would portray her work as untrustworthy and biased. Finding a title was difficult; "Silent Spring" was first proposed for a chapter on birds. By August 1961, Carson accepted her literary agent Marie Rodell’s suggestion that "Silent Spring" be a metaphorical title for the entire book, symbolizing a bleak future for the natural world. With Carson’s approval, editor Paul Brooks at Houghton Mifflin arranged illustrations by Louis and Lois Darling, who also designed the cover. The final writing included the first chapter, A Fable for Tomorrow, intended as a gentle introduction to a serious topic. By mid-1962, Brooks and Carson had completed editing and began sending the manuscript to select individuals for final feedback. Biographer Mark Hamilton Lytle notes that Carson deliberately wrote a book challenging the post-war American scientific paradigm of progress. The central theme of Silent Spring is the significant and often negative impact humans have on the natural world. Carson argues that pesticides have harmful environmental effects and should be called biocides because their effects extend beyond target pests; DDT is a prime example, and many synthetic pesticides are subject to bioaccumulation. She accuses the chemical industry of spreading disinformation and public officials of uncritically accepting industry claims. Most of the book focuses on pesticides’ effects on natural ecosystems, with four chapters detailing human pesticide poisoning, cancer, and other illnesses. Regarding DDT and cancer, Carson briefly notes that in animal tests, DDT produced suspicious liver tumors; FDA scientists were uncertain but felt there was "some justification for considering them low grade hepatic cell carcinomas," and Dr. Hueper now classifies DDT as a "chemical carcinogen." Carson predicted worsening consequences, especially as pests develop resistance and weakened ecosystems face invasive species. The book concludes with a call for a biotic approach to pest control as an alternative to chemical pesticides. Carson never called for a complete ban on DDT. She argued that even if DDT had no environmental side effects, its indiscriminate use would lead to resistance, rendering it ineffective in controlling target pests. She stated that while insect-borne diseases should not be ignored, it is not wise or responsible to use methods that worsen the problem, noting that efforts to control insects have often backfired, strengthening the pest population. She warned that "Malaria programmes are threatened by resistance among mosquitoes" and emphasized the advice from Holland’s Plant Protection Service: "Spray as little as you possibly can" rather than "Spray to the limit of your capacity," with pressure on pest populations always to be as slight as possible. Carson and the publication team expected fierce criticism and were particularly concerned about libel lawsuits. To prepare, they gathered prominent supporters before the book’s release. Most scientific chapters were reviewed by experts, and Carson found strong support. She attended the White House Conference on Conservation in May 1962; Houghton Mifflin distributed proof copies to delegates and promoted the upcoming New Yorker serialization. She also sent a proof copy to Supreme Court Associate Justice William O. Douglas, a long-time environmental advocate who had previously opposed the rejection of the Long Island pesticide spraying case and provided some of the material for her herbicide chapter. Pre-publication promotion generated interest, but the serialization in The New Yorker, beginning June 16, 1962, dramatically increased attention, bringing the book to the chemical industry, its lobbyists, and the general public. Around that time, Carson learned that Silent Spring had been selected as the Book of the Month for October, which she said would "carry it to farms and hamlets all over that country that don't know what a bookstore looks like—much less The New Yorker." Other publicity included a positive editorial in The New York Times and excerpts in Audubon, with additional coverage in July and August as chemical companies responded. The story of the thalidomide birth defect tragedy broke just before publication, prompting comparisons between Carson and Frances Oldham Kelsey, the FDA reviewer who blocked the drug’s sale. Critics attacked Carson personally, calling her a "bird and bunny lover" and, in the eyes of the chemical industry, a "woman out of control" for making claims about an industry outside traditional gender roles. In the weeks before the September 27, 1962, publication, the chemical industry strongly opposed the book. DuPont and Velsicol Chemical Corporation (exclusive manufacturer of chlordane and heptachlor) were among the first to respond; DuPont compiled a report on press coverage and estimated public impact, while Velsicol threatened legal action against Houghton Mifflin and The New Yorker and Audubon unless features were canceled. Industry representatives and lobbyists filed numerous non-specific complaints, some anonymously, and produced brochures and articles defending pesticide use. However, Carson and her legal team were confident in the book’s vetting process, and the publications proceeded as planned, including a Book-of-the-Month printing with a pamphlet endorsed by William O. Douglas. American Cyanamid biochemist Robert White-Stevens and former chemist Thomas Jukes were among the most aggressive critics, especially of Carson’s DDT analysis. White-Stevens claimed that following Carson’s advice would return society to the "Dark Ages," and others attacked her scientific credentials (due to her training in marine biology rather than biochemistry) and character, with White-Stevens calling her "a fanatic defender of the cult of the balance of nature" and former U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Ezra Taft Benson reportedly stating that because she was unmarried and physically attractive, she was "probably a Communist." Critics repeatedly claimed she advocated eliminating all pesticides, but Carson clarified she did not support banning or withdrawing helpful pesticides, but rather promoted responsible, carefully managed use with awareness of ecosystem impacts. She concluded her DDT section not with a ban but with advice to spray as little as possible to prevent resistance. The academic community, including H. J. Muller, Loren Eiseley, Clarence Cottam, and Frank Egler, largely supported the book’s scientific claims, and public opinion soon shifted in Carson’s favor. The chemical industry campaign backfired, as the controversy heightened public awareness of pesticide dangers and boosted book sales. Pesticide use became a major public issue, especially after the CBS Reports TV special The Silent Spring of Rachel Carson aired April 3, 1963, which included Carson reading from the book and interviews with critics like White-Stevens. According to biographer Linda Lear, in contrast to the "wild-eyed, loud-voiced" White-Stevens, Carson appeared anything but a hysterical alarmist. The estimated audience of ten to fifteen million responded overwhelmingly positively, leading to a congressional review of pesticide dangers and the release of a pesticide report by the President's Science Advisory Committee. Within a year, attacks on the book and Carson largely lost momentum. In one of her last public appearances, Carson testified before President John F. Kennedy’s Science Advisory Committee, which issued its report on May 15, 1963, largely supporting her claims. Following the report, she testified before a U.S. Senate subcommittee on policy recommendations. Though she received hundreds of speaking invitations, she declined most due to declining health, as her cancer progressed faster than radiation therapy, with only brief remissions. She spoke as much as possible, including on The Today Show and at several dinners in her honor. In late 1963, she received awards including the Audubon Medal, the Cullum Geographical Medal, and induction into the American Academy of Arts and Letters. In January 1964, Carson became ill with a respiratory virus; her condition worsened, and in February doctors found she had severe anemia from radiation treatments. In March, they discovered the cancer had spread to her liver. She died of a heart attack on April 14, 1964, in her home in Silver Spring, Maryland. Her body was cremated, and some ashes were buried beside her mother at Parklawn Memorial Gardens in Rockville, Maryland, while the rest were scattered along the coast of Squirrel Island near Sheepscot River in Maine. Carson bequeathed her manuscripts and papers to Yale University to take advantage of the Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library’s state-of-the-art preservation facilities. Her longtime agent and literary executor Marie Rodell spent nearly two years organizing and cataloging the papers and correspondence, distributing letters to their senders so only approved letters were submitted to the archive. In 1965, Rodell published an essay Carson intended to expand into a book: The Sense of Wonder, combined with photographs by Charles Pratt and others, urging parents to help children experience the "lasting pleasures of contact with the natural world ... available to anyone who will place himself under the influence of earth, sea, and sky and their amazing life." In 1998, a volume of Carson’s previously unpublished work, Lost Woods: The Discovered Writing of Rachel Carson, edited by Linda Lear, was published. All of Carson’s books remain in print. Her work had a powerful impact on the environmental movement, with Silent Spring serving as a rallying point for the 1960s social movement. Environmental engineer and Carson scholar H. Patricia Hynes states that Silent Spring "altered the balance of power in the world. No one since would be able to sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress so easily or uncritically." Carson’s work and the activism it inspired are at least partly responsible for the deep ecology movement and the strength of the grassroots environmental movement since the 1960s, and it influenced the rise of ecofeminism and many feminist scientists. While there is no evidence Carson was an openly active women’s rights activist, her work and its criticism have left an iconic legacy for ecofeminism. Attacks on her credibility included labeling her an "amateur" and claiming her writing was too "emotional." Ecofeminist scholars argue that dissenting rhetoric was gendered to portray her as hysterical because her arguments challenged capitalist agri-business. Others, such as Yaakov Garb, suggest Carson had no anti-capitalist agenda and that such attacks were unwarranted. The way photos of Carson were used to portray her—showing her in leisure activities rather than scientific work—is also questioned. Carson’s most direct legacy was the campaign to ban DDT in the United States and globally. Though environmental concerns about DDT had been considered as early as her testimony before the President’s Science Advisory Committee, the 1967 formation of the Environmental Defense Fund marked the first major milestone in the campaign. The organization brought lawsuits to "establish a citizen's right to a clean environment," using arguments similar to Carson’s. By 1972, the Environmental Defense Fund and other activist groups had succeeded in securing a phase-out of DDT.

Eminist scholars argue that the dissenting rhetoric directed at Rachel Carson was not only gendered, portraying her as hysterical, but also stemmed from her challenging the capitalist production of large agri-business corporations. Others, like Yaakov Garb, contend that Carson was neither a women's rights activist nor committed to an anti-capitalist agenda, suggesting such criticisms were unfounded. The portrayal of Carson in photographs is also questioned, as few depict her engaged in scientific work, instead showing her in leisure activities. Carson's most significant legacy in the environmental movement was the campaign to ban DDT in the United States and globally. Although environmental concerns about DDT were considered as early as her testimony before the President's Science Advisory Committee, the 1967 formation of the Environmental Defense Fund marked the first major step in the campaign, as it brought lawsuits to establish a citizen's right to a clean environment using arguments closely aligned with Carson's. By 1972, the Environmental Defense Fund and other activist groups had achieved a phase-out of DDT use in the U.S. (except in emergencies). The Nixon Administration created the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in 1970, addressing Carson’s concern that the USDA, which previously regulated pesticides and promoted agriculture, had a conflict of interest by not considering environmental or wildlife impacts. Fifteen years later, a journalist described the EPA as "the extended shadow of Silent Spring," and much of its early work, including enforcing the 1972 Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act, directly followed Carson’s efforts. In the 1980s, the Reagan Administration prioritized economic growth and rolled back many environmental policies established in response to Carson’s work. Since her death, numerous groups including government bodies, environmental organizations, and scholarly societies have honored Carson. On June 9, 1980, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor in the U.S. A 17¢ Great Americans postage stamp was issued the following year, and several other countries have since issued stamps in her honor. In 1973, she was inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame. In 2016, the University of California, Santa Cruz renamed its College Eight Rachel Carson College, becoming the first college at the university to bear a woman’s name. The Munich Rachel Carson Center for Environment and Society was founded in 2009 as a joint initiative of Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität and the Deutsches Museum, supported by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research. Carson’s birthplace and childhood home in Springdale, Pennsylvania, is now a National Register of Historic Places site, managed by the Rachel Carson Homestead Association since 1975. Her home in Colesville, Maryland, where she wrote Silent Spring, was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1991. A 46.1-mile (74 km) hiking trail near Pittsburgh, the Rachel Carson Trail, was dedicated in 1975 and maintained by the Rachel Carson Trails Conservancy; a bridge in Pittsburgh was renamed the Rachel Carson Bridge, and the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection’s State Office Building in Harrisburg is also named after her. Elementary schools in Gaithersburg, Maryland, Sammamish, Washington, and San Jose, California, and middle schools in Beaverton, Oregon, Queens, New York City, Herndon, Virginia, and Brooklyn, New York City, have been named in her honor. Two research vessels bear her name: one on the west coast, owned by Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI), and another on the east coast, operated by the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science; a former naval vessel converted by the U.S. EPA, now scrapped, operated on the Great Lakes, and the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary operates a mooring buoy maintenance vessel named the Rachel Carson. The ceremonial auditorium at the EPA headquarters, the William Jefferson Clinton Federal Building, is named the Rachel Carson Room, located near the EPA Administrator’s office and hosting key announcements such as the Clean Air Interstate Rule. Conservation areas named for Carson include the 650-acre (263 ha) Rachel Carson Conservation Park in Montgomery County, Maryland, acquired between 1964 and 1990 and administered by the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission; the Coastal Maine National Wildlife Refuge, renamed the Rachel Carson National Wildlife Refuge in 1969, with future expansions reaching about 9,125 acres (3,693 ha); and a reserve in Beaufort, North Carolina, renamed in her honor in 1985. Carson is frequently honored through prizes: the Rachel Carson Prize, founded in Stavanger, Norway in 1991, recognizes women for contributions to environmental protection; the American Society for Environmental History awards the Rachel Carson Prize for Best Dissertation since 1993; since 1998, the Society for Social Studies of Science has awarded the annual Rachel Carson Book Prize for works of social or political relevance in science and technology studies; the Society of Environmental Journalists gives annual awards and honorable mentions for environmental books in Carson’s name, such as Joe Roman’s Listed: Dispatches from America's Endangered Species Act in 2012; the Sierra Club recognizes estate donors as the Rachel Carson Society; and the Rachel Carson Center at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München awards post-doctoral fellowships in environmental and societal studies. A Rachel Carson sculpture in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, was unveiled on July 14, 2013. Google created a Doodle for her 107th birthday on May 27, 2014. She was featured in U2’s "HerStory" video tribute during their 2017 tour for the 30th anniversary of The Joshua Tree, during a performance of "Ultraviolet (Light My Way)" from the 1991 album Achtung Baby. In 2019, Time selected Carson for its 1963 women of the year cover in a series of 89 new covers celebrating women from 1920 onward. The centennial of her birth in 2007 was marked on Earth Day (April 22) with the release of "Courage for the Earth: Writers, Scientists, and Activists Celebrate the Life and Writing of Rachel Carson," a collection of 13 essays by environmental writers and scientists. Democratic Senator Benjamin L. Cardin of Maryland had planned to introduce a resolution honoring Carson for her "legacy of scientific rigor coupled with poetic sensibility" on the 100th anniversary of her birth, but it was blocked by Republican Senator Tom Coburn of Oklahoma. On May 27, 2007, the Rachel Carson Homestead Association hosted a birthday party and sustainable feast at her home in Springdale, Pennsylvania, and the first Rachel Carson Legacy Conference in Pittsburgh, with E. O. Wilson as keynote speaker; both events continue annually. In 2007, American author Ginger Wadsworth published a biography of Carson.
